import parse

# Test precision without alignment
tests = [
    ('{:.2}', 'look', 'lo'),
    ('{:2}', 'look', 'lo'),
    ('{:4}{}', 'look at that', ('look', ' at that')),
    ('{:4}{:.4}', 'look at that', ('look at ', 'that')),
]

for pattern, string, expected in tests:
    p = parse.compile(pattern)
    r = p.parse(string)
    status = "✓" if r and r.fixed == expected else "✗"
    print(f"{status} {pattern!r} on {string!r}: got {r.fixed if r else None}, expected {expected}")
    if r:
        print(f"   expr={p._expression!r}")
PYEOF

raw_message.reasoning:
Now I understand the precision behavior better:
- `{:.2}` means "match up to 2 characters" (precision is a maximum)
- `{:2}` means "match at least 2 characters" (width is a minimum)
- `{:4.4}` means "match exactly 4 characters"

Looking at line 931: `res = parse.parse('{:4}{:.4}', 'look at that')` gives `('look at ', 'that')`. So `{:4}` matches at least 4 chars ("look at ") and `{:.4}` matches up to 4 chars ("that").
